questions.prompt: A retrained model is canaried with analysis on HTTP error rate and p95 latency. A feature is computed with the wrong sign at serving time, so a third of its answers are wrong. What does the canary analysis do?
choices: It aborts, because wrong answers raise the error rate
It aborts, because a wrong model is slower to compute
It promotes the model: every answer is a fast, valid 200, so neither metric moves
It pauses for a human, because the analysis is Inconclusive
questions.explanation: Errors and latency describe whether the service answered, not whether the answer was right. A wrong model answers 200 as fast as a right one. A model rollout needs a quality proxy: agreement with the current model during a shadow, a feedback or conversion rate, or delayed labels.

questions.prompt: The router mirrors every request to a shadow model, and the shadow starts hanging for 30 seconds per call. What happens to the users' responses in minirollout?
choices: Nothing: the copy goes onto a bounded queue after the primary answered, workers call the shadow, and when the queue is full mirror jobs are dropped and counted
Responses wait for the shadow up to the timeout, then the primary's answer is returned
The router switches users to the shadow's answer when the primary is slower
The router returns 503 until the shadow recovers, to protect the comparison
questions.explanation: A shadow must never change or delay a response. minirollout records the served answer, then calls put_nowait on a bounded queue; two workers call the shadow. A hanging shadow fills the queue and further copies are dropped (mirror_dropped), while callers see the primary's latency. Gateway API's RequestMirror has the same rule: the mirror's response must be ignored.

questions.prompt: Why does minirollout assign canary users with a salted hash of the user ID instead of a random number per request?
choices: Hashing is faster than generating random numbers
Random numbers cannot produce a weight of exactly 10%
Kubernetes Services require a hash to route by user
A user keeps one version for the whole rollout, raising the weight only adds users, feedback can be attributed to one version, and a new salt per candidate picks a different first cohort
questions.explanation: bucket(user, salt) is a fixed number between 0 and 100 per user, so the same user always lands on the same side, and bucket < 10 implies bucket < 50. A per-request split gives one user two models on two refreshes and makes their feedback meaningless. Service, HTTPRoute and KServe weights are per connection or per request, so stickiness needs a cohort decision such as a header set from the same kind of hash.

questions.prompt: An Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate uses the web provider with jsonPath {$} and both successCondition and failureCondition start with result.candidate.feedback >= 150. The first measurement sees 90 feedback answers from the canary. What happens?
choices: The measurement fails, because 90 is below 150
The measurement is Inconclusive, because neither condition is true, and the Rollout pauses for a human instead of deciding on too little data
The measurement is Successful, because a web metric without enough data defaults to success
The measurement is an Error, because jsonPath {$} is not allowed
questions.explanation: With both conditions set, a value that satisfies neither is Inconclusive, and an Inconclusive run pauses the Rollout. Guarding both conditions with the sample count turns 'too few samples' into a hold, which is minirollout's hold verdict. jsonPath {$} is the default and makes the whole JSON response available as result.

questions.prompt: Over a day, a canary collects 40,000 feedback answers per side. Its positive rate is 96.6% against the primary's 97.0%, and the two-proportion z-test gives p = 0.001. The plan set alpha 0.01 and a minimum quality drop of 5 points. What should the analysis decide?
choices: Roll back, because p is below alpha
Hold, because a significant difference needs a human
Roll back, because any drop in quality is unacceptable for a model
Promote: the drop is real but 0.4 points, far below the 5-point minimum effect that was chosen as worth acting on
questions.explanation: With enough samples every difference becomes significant. A rollback needs both a p-value under alpha and an effect above the minimum effect decided in advance; otherwise any large rollout would roll back on noise-sized differences. The minimum effect is a product decision; the sample size needed to detect it follows from it.

questions.prompt: A service gets 20 requests per second. The plan canaries a model at 5%, needs 556 feedback answers per side to detect a 5-point drop, and every analysis looks at the last 20 seconds of samples. Every request gets feedback. What happens at the analysis step?
choices: It holds until it times out: a 20-second window holds about 20 canary answers, never 556, so the window must cover about 9 minutes, the weight must grow, or a shadow at 100% must provide the comparison
It promotes after 20 seconds, because no failure was seen
It rolls back, because 20 answers are too few to pass
It decides after 556 seconds, because each second adds one sample per side
questions.explanation: Time to a decision is the samples needed divided by the candidate's request rate: 556 / (20 x 0.05) is about 9 minutes, and a sliding window must be long enough to hold them, or the analysis can never leave hold. minirollout plan prints this and warns when the window cannot reach min-samples. A shadow at 100% reaches the same sample count in under a minute with no user exposed, but it measures agreement, not feedback.
